new_statements.quote: Signs in DGS are mono- or disyllabic [...] The syllable and a DGS prosodic word mostly coincide. The movement represents the nucleus of a syllable in DGS. [...] In case of disyllabic syllables and an expressed emphatic marking, there is a tendency to show a stress pattern on the first syllable. a. EXAM (disyllabic, reduplicated, stressed on first syllable) b. TABLE (disyllabic, different movements, stressed on first syllable) [...] 2.1.2. Foot: Due to the fact that signs are at most disyllabic in DGS [Phonology 2.1.1.], this part of the prosodic organization is not relevant in DGS.

new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (341 pp., text layer, pdfinfo Title 'A Grammar of German Sign Language (DGS)', eds. Proske, Herrmann, Hosemann & Steinbach, SIGN-HUB 2020, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Locator verified: Part 2 Phonology, Chapter 2 Prosody (authorship information: Annika Herrmann), 2.1.1 Syllable on PDF p.67 running onto p.68, 2.1.2 Foot on p.68 — exactly as the report states. extracted text of pp.67-68 reads: 'Signs in DGS are mono- or disyllabic and show different combinations of these units such as HMH... The syllable and a DGS prosodic word mostly coincide. The movement represents the nucleus of a syllable in DGS. Single movements are light syllables... whereas combinations of movements... carry more…
new_statements.rule_in_words: DGS signs are at most disyllabic (syllable = hold/movement sequence) and the syllable usually coincides with the prosodic word; when a disyllabic sign is produced with emphatic prominence, the stress tends to fall on the first syllable (first movement). Prominence is realized manually (lengthening, tense articulation, velocity) and non-manually.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None discussed; foot level declared not relevant because signs are at most disyllabic.
new_statements.exceptions: Stated only as a 'tendency' under emphatic marking; no lexical exceptions given. Elsewhere: pronominal subject copies are unstressed (Syntax 2.6.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical sign / prosodic word level in a sign language; 'stress' = visual prominence on one of at most two movement-syllables, observed under emphatic marking. Not spoken word stress; catalogers may prefer to code as sign-language prominence with first-syllable tendency.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes DGS as a whole (germ1281); Prosody chapter data from one deaf native consultant from Northern Germany. Note this is a sign language: 'syllable' = hold/movement sequence, 'stress' = manual/non-manual prominence (lengthening, tense articulation, velocity) on a sign; signs are at most disyllabic, so the statement concerns which of two movements/syllables carries emphatic prominence, not spoken-language word stress.

sources.note: Phonology Ch.2 Prosody §2.1.1 Syllable (PDF pp.67-68): signs are mono- or disyllabic; syllable and prosodic word mostly coincide; for disyllabic signs with emphatic marking there is a tendency to a stress pattern on the first syllable (EXAM, TABLE 'stressed on first syllable'); §2.1.2 Foot not relevant since signs are at most disyllabic; §2.1 prominence marked by lengthening, tense articulation, velocity changes and non-manuals. Also Syntax: pronoun copy is 'unstressed'.
